titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive manifest supplies an empty title text, which is preserved exactly. Its source page has malformed raw HTML around a continuation resembling the localized exchange “¿Quieres sentirte viejo?” “Sí.”; that broken continuation is documented rather than substituted for the manifest value. The official English title text is preserved exactly. The 1480×5246 Spanish raster was checked manually against the official 2× raster. OCR omitted DIOS MÍO, VALE, FWOOSH, HISSSSSS, the English signs and book title, misread many low-contrast lines, and fused or split several words. The authored transcript preserves three BIIIP sounds, CÁAAANCER, UEEEEEEE, NNNNNGGGGH, the visible truncated TAM, the partly occluded but determinate MONTAÑA, and the line-wrapped ARTICULACIONES. Tiny indeterminate poster, notice, book-byline, and chart marks are omitted; illustration icons are not textual units.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In health care, antecedentes are earlier conditions, diagnoses, or events that help a clinician assess the present situation.

example.en: The doctor reviewed my medical history.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: An articulación is the place where bones meet and movement can occur.

example.es: El frío le molesta en las articulaciones.
example.en: The cold bothers her joints.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Biiip imitates a sustained electronic tone. Spanish sound spellings vary, and extra i letters make the tone feel longer.

example.en: The device went beep.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: cancer, pronounced with an exaggerated long vowel
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The standard word is cáncer. Extra a letters show that the stressed vowel is being drawn out for comic emphasis; the written accent stays on the first á.

example.en: The ordinary word is cancer.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Calva describes a woman or feminine noun with no hair. The masculine form is calvo.

example.es: La actriz aparece calva en la escena.
example.en: The actress appears bald in the scene.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to care for; to look after
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cuidar can be followed by de when it means taking responsibility for a person, animal, or thing.

example.es: Voy a cuidar de las plantas.
example.en: I am going to take care of the plants.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dados is the masculine plural form of dado when it introduces several facts or circumstances to be considered.

example.en: Given the prices, we will buy less.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dedo can mean either a finger or a toe. The surrounding context or the addition del pie makes the body part clear.

example.es: Me hice daño en un dedo del pie.
example.en: I hurt one of my toes.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you got; you gave yourself (in darse un golpe)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Diste is a completed-past form of dar for one familiar listener. With te and un golpe, it says that the listener bumped or hurt themself.

example.es: Te diste un golpe en la rodilla.
example.en: You bumped your knee.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Duele is used when one thing causes pain. The person feeling it is marked with me, te, le, nos, os, or les.

example.en: My back hurts.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Estimaron is the completed-past form of estimar for a plural subject.

example.en: They estimated the cost yesterday.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Fwoosh is a comic sound effect for a fast rush through air or water.

example.es: El objeto cayó con un fwoosh.
example.en: The object fell with a fwoosh.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: A golpe is a sudden impact. In darse un golpe, it commonly refers to bumping or hurting oneself.

example.es: Oí un golpe en la puerta.
example.en: I heard a knock at the door.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Gordo normally means fat or thick. In the body-part name dedo gordo, it identifies the big toe.

example.en: The big toe is swollen.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hicieron is the irregular completed-past form of hacer for a plural subject.

example.en: They asked several questions.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hissssss imitates a sustained hiss. Repeated s letters make the sound last longer on the page.

example.en: The snake went hiss.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Llamaremos keeps the full verb llamar and adds the -emos future ending for nosotros.

example.en: We will call you tomorrow.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Madrugar means getting up very early, usually because the day or an obligation starts early.

example.en: Tomorrow we have to get up early.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Metástasis is the medical term for disease spreading from its original site to another part of the body.

example.en: The tests showed no metastasis.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: my; part of the exclamation madre mía
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Mía is the feminine singular possessive form matching madre. In ¡Madre mía!, the whole expression is a reaction rather than a literal statement about one's mother.

example.en: Goodness, what a lot of noise!

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In Spain, a napolitana is a flaky rectangular pastry commonly filled with chocolate or cream.

example.en: She bought a chocolate-filled pastry.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Necesite is a present subjunctive form of necesitar. The subjunctive is a special verb form used after puede que when the need is only a possibility.

example.en: He may need help.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: This drawn-out sound effect represents hesitation or reluctant agreement. Repeated letters stretch the groan.

example.en: She answered with a reluctant groan.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Optimista has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; optimistas is plural.

example.en: They made optimistic calculations.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Parezco is the yo form of parecer. With me and a, parecerse a means to resemble someone or something.

example.en: I look like my sister.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Preocuparte combines preocupar with te, the matching marker for one familiar listener. The marker attaches to the end of the verb's dictionary form.

example.en: You do not have to worry.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Seguramente often presents something as highly likely without making it completely certain.

example.en: She will probably arrive this afternoon.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Síntoma is grammatically masculine despite ending in -a: el síntoma, los síntomas.

example.en: The symptoms disappeared.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: socialized; accustomed to social contact (masculine plural)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Socializados describes people or animals that have learned to interact comfortably with others.

example.en: The puppies are well socialized.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tam is not a complete standard Spanish word. When the remaining letters are hidden or cut off, it can be the readable beginning of también.

example.en: We also want to go.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tarda is a present form of tardar for one person or thing. Tardar en followed by an action says that the action takes time.

example.en: The train takes a while to arrive.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: The written accent distinguishes té, the drink, from te, a short pronoun meaning you or to you.

example.en: We drink tea with lemon.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ueeeeeee represents an excited cry during fast or playful movement. The repeated e letters stretch the sound.

example.en: She shouted “wheee!” on the way down.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to come; to come over (addressing several people)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Veniros is venir plus os, the marker for informal plural vosotros in Spain. After tenéis que, it stays in this unchanged action form.

example.en: You all have to come over this summer.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Viene is the present form of venir for one subject. In a phrase such as el mes que viene, the coming month is the next one.

example.es: Nos mudamos el mes que viene.
example.en: We are moving next month.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: like; required after parecerse before the comparison
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Parecerse uses a before the person or thing that someone resembles.

example.es: El niño se parece a su abuelo.
example.en: The boy looks like his grandfather.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Camino can be a physical path or, figuratively, a long process that leads to a result.

example.es: Fue un camino largo y difícil.
example.en: It was a long and difficult journey.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Completo describes something that covers all the needed parts or the whole scope.

example.en: We need a full report.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Costar can describe difficulty rather than price. In cuesta followed by an action verb, the action is hard to do.

example.en: It is hard to admit a mistake.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: for; fixed link in ir/venir de visita
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In ir de visita or venir de visita, de connects the movement verb to visita. Natural English usually translates the whole expression as going or coming for a visit.

example.en: My aunt and uncle are coming for a visit.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: When cuidar means looking after someone or something, de introduces the person or thing receiving care.

example.en: She takes care of her dog.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de cerca, “up close”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: De is fixed before cerca when describing a close viewing distance.

example.en: I want to see it up close.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; links tardar to the action that takes time
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tardar uses en before an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: She took an hour to reply.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they are (in a state or condition)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Están is the present form of estar for a plural subject. Estar commonly describes a current condition.

example.en: The children are calm.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: we become (as part of nos hacemos + description)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Nos hacemos uses a form of hacer with nos to describe a gradual or chosen change. The following word names the new state.

example.es: Con los años nos hacemos más pacientes.
example.en: Over the years we become more patient.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses hacer una foto where English uses “take a photo.” Hago is the yo form of hacer.

example.es: Le hago una foto al edificio.
example.en: I take a photo of the building.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: bad; badly (in ni tan mal, “not so bad”)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Mal supplies the negative evaluation in ni tan mal, a conversational way to say that something turned out reasonably well.

example.es: El resultado no fue perfecto, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: The result was not perfect, but not too bad.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: not; begins ni tan mal, “not so bad”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In the conversational expression ni tan mal, ni helps soften or reverse the negative evaluation rather than joining a list.

example.es: Llegamos tarde, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: We arrived late, but it was not too bad.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Perdiendo is the ongoing-action form of perder. After a form of estar, it presents the loss as in progress.

example.en: I am losing patience.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Señal can name a posted sign, a transmitted signal, or evidence that points to a condition.

example.es: La fiebre puede ser una señal de infección.
example.en: A fever can be a sign of infection.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: yourself; marks the listener in darse un golpe
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In te diste un golpe, te marks one familiar listener as the person who experienced the bump. Natural English often uses “yourself” or rearranges the body part.

example.en: Did you bump yourself?

cardDefinitions.noteEn: As a noun, visita names an occasion when someone comes to see another person or place; it is not the verb form “visits.”

example.en: The visit lasted two days.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I am going to (before a + action)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Voy is the yo form of ir. Before a and an action verb, voy a announces a plan or near-future action.

example.en: I am going to rest.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say “next year” by describing the year that is coming?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The relative word que links año to viene, “comes.” The same pattern works with other time nouns: la semana que viene and el mes que viene. Viene stays singular because it describes one week, month, or year.

example.en: We will start next year.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone goes or comes for a visit?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of ir or venir followed by de visita.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Only ir or venir changes for the person and time. The fixed words de visita identify the purpose as visiting, and natural English usually supplies “for a visit.”

example.en: Our friends are coming for a visit.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use dedo gordo; add del pie when the context does not make the foot clear.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dedo can mean either finger or toe. Gordo literally means fat or thick, but dedo gordo is the conventional name for the big toe. The adjective changes if the noun changes: dedos gordos for more than one.

example.es: Me lesioné el dedo gordo del pie.
example.en: I injured my big toe.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone bumps or hurts themself?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching form of darse followed by un golpe.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Darse uses me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person who experiences the impact. Dar changes for the person and time; un golpe stays as the impact being experienced.

example.es: Luis se dio un golpe en el brazo.
example.en: Luis bumped his arm.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you introduce facts or circumstances as things to consider?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put dado, dada, dados, or dadas before the noun and make it match that noun.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In this pattern, dado means “given” or “considering,” not “die” or “dice.” It behaves like a describing word: dado el tiempo, dada la situación, dados los precios, dadas las circunstancias.

example.en: Given the circumstances, we will wait.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that one person or thing resembles another?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching small pronoun, a form of parecer, then a and the comparison target.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The small pronoun changes with the person: me parezco, te pareces, se parece, nos parecemos. Parecer also changes for the person and time, while a always introduces who or what provides the comparison.

example.es: Esta casa se parece a la nuestra.
example.en: This house resembles ours.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is sufficiently described in a certain way?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put lo bastante before the describing word.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Lo bastante means “enough” or “sufficiently” before a description. Lo and bastante stay unchanged; the adjective still matches the person or thing described, as in lo bastante alta or lo bastante preparados.

example.es: Las cajas son lo bastante grandes.
example.en: The boxes are large enough.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes care of a person, animal, or thing?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of cuidar followed by de and the person or thing receiving care.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cuidar changes for the person and time. De introduces what is being looked after: cuido de, cuidamos de, cuidará de.

example.en: Marta takes care of her grandfather.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is seen or examined up close?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the fixed expression de cerca.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: De cerca describes a close viewing or observing distance. Keep both words together; cerca de has the different meaning “near” and normally introduces a following place, person, or thing.

example.es: Quiero mirar el mapa de cerca.
example.en: I want to look at the map up close.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What common exclamation can express surprise, shock, or amazement?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The words literally mean “my mother,” but speakers often use the complete expression as a reaction without referring to their mother. Tone and context determine whether it sounds alarmed, impressed, or overwhelmed.

example.en: Goodness, what a storm!

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say conversationally that something is actually not too bad?
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This informal expression gives a restrained positive assessment: the result may not be perfect, but it is acceptable or better than expected. It often stands alone after a pause or contrast.

example.es: No ganamos, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: We did not win, but it was not too bad.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone loses their sight?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of perder followed by la vista.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish normally uses the definite article la in this expression even when English uses “one's” or a possessive. Perder changes for the person and time; la vista stays fixed as the ability to see.

example.es: La enfermedad puede hacerle perder la vista.
example.en: The illness can cause him to lose his sight.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that doing an action is difficult or takes effort?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of costar followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: When an action is the difficult thing, costar is normally singular: cuesta for the present, costó for a completed past event, or costará for the future. The following action stays in its basic form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: It is hard to stay calm.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that no trace or sign of something can be found?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use sin rastro de followed by the thing that cannot be found.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Rastro can literally mean a trail or trace. In this expression, sin rastro de says that no evidence remains. Before el, de contracts to del: sin rastro del problema.

example.es: La playa quedó sin rastro de basura.
example.en: The beach was left with no trace of litter.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: dos años · siete años · diez años · quince años
cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why does the strip revisit scenes separated by two, seven, ten, and fifteen years?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: It presents a long cancer-survival retrospective, moving from treatment and uncertainty toward fifteen years without a recurrence.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The grayscale panels reprise earlier stages of diagnosis, treatment, recurrence anxiety, and milestones. The newer scenes add ordinary shared life, aging, and care. The final fifteen-year marker makes survival itself—not a conventional punch line—the emotional culmination.
